ai.definition: Minimal & Synthetic Genomes involve creating cells with either the smallest possible genome or a fully rewritten one. This technology aims to understand the essential genes required for life by reducing complexity and studying the core functions necessary for cellular survival.
ai.howItWorks: Genomes are synthesized chemically or trimmed gene-by-gene through genetic engineering techniques. The process involves identifying and removing non-essential genes while ensuring that the remaining genes can support cell viability. This is achieved using computational models, experimental biology, and iterative refinement to determine the minimal set of genes required for a cell to function.
ai.problemSolved: Understanding the fundamental requirements for life at the genetic level, enabling the creation of simpler organisms with potential applications in biotechnology and medicine.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves chemical synthesis of DNA sequences, followed by their integration into bacterial or yeast cells. This can be done through electroporation, conjugation, or other gene transfer methods.
ai.buildProcess: Genomes are built using a combination of computational design to predict minimal sets and experimental validation to test the viability of these designs in living organisms. The process often involves iterative cycles of genome reduction, transplantation into host cells, and functional testing.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the complexity of chemical synthesis, the need for specialized equipment and reagents, and the labor-intensive nature of genetic engineering and cell culture.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: promising but early-stage with potential for significant advancements in biotechnology and medicine
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations targeting minimal & synthetic genomes. However, broader regulations on genetically modified organisms (GMOs) may apply.
ai.profitability: Not yet commercially viable but has potential for future applications in biotechnology and pharmaceuticals
ai.futureDevelopment: Further research is needed to optimize minimal genome designs, improve synthesis techniques, and explore practical applications. Collaboration between academia and industry will likely drive progress.

glossary.def: A set of genes that are essential for the survival and reproduction of a cell.
An interdisciplinary field combining biology, engineering, and computer science to design and construct new biological parts, devices, and systems.
The process of creating artificial DNA sequences in the laboratory using chemical methods.

subsystems.name: Genome design layer
subsystems.role: software that specifies which genes stay, which go, and in what order.

subsystems.name: DNA synthesis and assembly
subsystems.role: turns the design into physical DNA, from short pieces up to whole chromosomes.
parts: yeast or bacterial hosts for stitching large fragments

subsystems.name: Delivery and transplantation
subsystems.role: gets a genome-sized piece of DNA into a living cell.

subsystems.name: Minimisation analysis
subsystems.role: finds out which of the genes are genuinely needed.

subsystems.name: Chassis cell
subsystems.role: the host organism whose genome is being rebuilt or trimmed.

subsystems.name: Verification
subsystems.role: proves the written sequence matches the living cell.

buildSteps.title: Pick a chassis
buildSteps.detail: Start with an organism that grows fast and has a naturally small genome, so the target is tractable.

buildSteps.title: Design the genome on a computer
buildSteps.detail: Annotate every gene, mark the ones known to be essential, strip out the rest, rewrite codons to a chosen set, and insert harmless watermark sequences so the synthetic DNA can be told apart from natural DNA.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise short DNA
buildSteps.detail: Build the sequence chemically as many thousands of short oligonucleotides, a few hundred bases each.

buildSteps.title: Assemble into longer pieces
buildSteps.detail: Join the oligonucleotides in vitro into cassettes of a few thousand base pairs, then correct errors before scaling up further.

buildSteps.title: Stitch in a living carrier
buildSteps.detail: Combine cassettes step by step inside yeast, which tolerates very large foreign DNA, until a complete genome of around half a million to several million base pairs is assembled.

buildSteps.title: Transplant or replace
buildSteps.detail: Move the finished genome into a recipient cell that has had its own DNA removed, or swap it into a native chromosome segment by segment, as in the synthetic yeast projects.

buildSteps.title: Boot the cell
buildSteps.detail: Select for cells in which the synthetic genome takes over and drives normal growth and division; sequence them to confirm nothing was lost.

buildSteps.title: Trim to the minimum
buildSteps.detail: Scramble genes one at a time with transposons to test which can be deleted; the smallest bacterial cell built this way carried 473 genes, and roughly a third of those still have no known function.

buildSteps.title: Test as a chassis
buildSteps.detail: Once the gene set is known and stable, add engineered pathways on top to see whether a minimal cell is a more predictable factory than a natural one.

prerequisites.why: cost per base pair has fallen enormously, but assembling millions of error-free base pairs is still slow and expensive.
without cheap, fast reading of DNA you cannot check that the synthesised genome is correct.
moving a whole genome into a cell has been done in a few bacterial species, not routinely.
you can only delete what you know is dispensable; a large share of minimal-cell genes are still unexplained.
cells built from scratch remove natural barriers, so engineering controls must replace them.

pathway.milestone: a viable bacterial cell running on a chemically synthesised genome of 473 genes; individual synthetic chromosomes running inside yeast
pathway.unlocks: proof that a genome can be written rather than copied.

pathway.milestone: a wholly synthetic eukaryotic genome, with a yeast cell carrying entirely man-made chromosomes
pathway.unlocks: design rules for larger, more complex cells.

pathway.milestone: streamlined industrial chassis with no unexplained genes and built-in virus resistance through codon recoding
pathway.unlocks: fermentation that is easier to control and harder to infect.

pathway.milestone: genomes designed for specified functions, with robust safety and screening rules
pathway.unlocks: predictable engineered cells — and a serious governance problem to solve alongside them.
